mainTopic: The verse of the seven species as an אסמכתא for שיעורין, and whether שיעורין and חציצין are הלכה למשה מסיני
overview: Our amud continues a list built on the verse 'ארץ חטה ושעורה וגפן ותאנה ורמון ארץ זית שמן ודבש'. Each food in the verse is linked to a halachic measurement (שיעור). חטה is the time of אכילת פרס in a בית המנוגע, measured with wheat bread. שעורה is a barley-sized bone of a מת, גפן is a רביעית of wine for a נזיר, and תאנה is a גרוגרת for carrying on שבת. רמון is a pomegranate-sized hole in a vessel, זית shows that most measurements are a כזית, and דבש is a large date for eating on יום הכפורים. The גמרא then asks whether this list proves the שיעורין are written Torah law, against רב's statement that they are הלכה למשה מסיני. It answers that the sizes are not actually written in the verse: they are a tradition from סיני, and the verse is only an אסמכתא. Next the גמרא challenges רב's claim about חציצין, since a verse already teaches that nothing may block the water during immersion. It first answers that the tradition is about knotted hair, following רבה בר בר חנה. When hair also turns out to be included in the verse, the גמרא begins a new answer based on רבי יצחק, whose words continue on the next amud.

steps.title: A person wearing his clothes in a בית המנוגע: he is impure at once, his clothes only after a delay
steps.stepSummary: The source about בית המנוגע continues. If a person enters wearing his clothes, sandals, and rings, he becomes טמא immediately. The items he is wearing stay טהור until he stays inside for the time it takes to eat a פרס.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he was wearing his clothes, with his sandals on his feet and his rings on his fingers, he becomes impure immediately. But the clothes, sandals, and rings stay pure until he stays inside long enough to eat half a loaf.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is continuing the source it quoted to explain the word חטה in the verse. This line covers the case where the person's things are on his body, not just being carried.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person's own body becomes טמא the moment he walks into the בית המנוגע. Things he is wearing are treated differently: they become טמא only after a fixed amount of time, the time of אכילת פרס. That time measurement is the link to חטה, as the next step explains.

keyTerms.meaning: A house struck with צרעת, which makes people and objects inside it impure
The time it takes to eat a פרס (half a loaf); a standard halachic time measure

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the person and his clothes. The person becomes impure immediately. Only the items he is wearing wait for the אכילת פרס time.

phrases.english: If he was dressed in his clothes
and his sandals were on his feet
and his rings were on his fingers
he is impure immediately
phrases.notes: His body becomes impure upon entering.

phrases.english: but they (the clothes, sandals, rings) are pure
until he stays long enough to eat half a loaf
phrases.notes: פרס = half a loaf. This time measure is what links the case to חטה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the source about בית המנוגע that the גמרא began quoting (on the previous amud) to explain חטה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person entering a בית המנוגע becomes טמא at once. The clothes and jewelry he is wearing become טמא only after he stays the time of אכילת פרס.

steps.title: The אכילת פרס time is measured with wheat bread eaten reclining with a relish
steps.stepSummary: The source defines the אכילת פרס time: it uses wheat bread, not barley bread, eaten while reclining with a condiment. This is the reason the case is tied to חטה (wheat).
steps.simpleTranslation: The measure uses wheat bread and not barley bread, eaten by someone reclining and eating it with a relish.
steps.whatsHappening: The source spells out exactly how to measure the time of אכילת פרס. This finishes the explanation of how חטה in the verse hints to a שיעור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wheat bread is eaten faster than barley bread, and eating with a relish while reclining is faster still. So the time is the shortest normal eating time. Because the measure is based specifically on wheat, the verse's word חטה is read as a hint to this שיעור.

keyTerms.meaning: Reclining, the normal relaxed way of eating a meal
A relish or condiment eaten with bread

steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why the word חטה in the verse fits: the time-שיעור of אכילת פרס is defined by wheat bread.

phrases.english: wheat bread and not barley bread
phrases.notes: Wheat bread is eaten faster, so the time is shorter.

phrases.english: reclining and eating it with relish
phrases.notes: Eating with a condiment speeds up eating.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the אכילת פרס measurement mentioned in step 1 and ties it to חטה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The אכילת פרס time is measured by wheat bread, eaten reclining with a relish, so it is a שיעור connected to חטה.

steps.title: Barley hints to the barley-sized bone of a dead body
steps.stepSummary: The verse's word שעורה hints to the rule that a bone from a dead body the size of a barley grain transmits טומאה by touching and carrying, but not through אהל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Barley: as we learned in a משנה, a bone the size of a barley grain makes things impure by touching and by carrying, but it does not make things impure through a tent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next word in the verse, שעורה, and quotes a משנה showing a שיעור measured by barley.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A tiny bone from a מת, only the size of a barley grain, still has some power of טומאה: מגע (touch) and משא (carrying). It is too small for טומאת אהל, which means it does not make everything under the same roof impure. Since the size is measured by a barley grain, the word שעורה hints to it.

keyTerms.meaning: A bone the size of a barley grain
Impurity passed by touching and by carrying
Impurity spread to everything under the same roof as a dead body

steps.confusionAlert: This bone does make things impure, just not in every way. It passes טומאה through touch and carrying, but not through אהל.

phrases.english: Barley — as we learned in a mishna:
a bone the size of a barley grain
imparts impurity through contact and carrying
but does not impart impurity through a tent

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from חטה to the next species in the verse, שעורה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bone of a מת the size of a barley grain transmits טומאה by מגע and משא but not by אהל, and the verse's שעורה hints to this.

steps.title: The vine hints to a רביעית of wine for a נזיר
steps.stepSummary: The verse's word גפן hints to the שיעור of a רביעית of wine, the amount that makes a נזיר liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Vine: the amount of a רביעית of wine for a נזיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next word in the verse, גפן, and gives the שיעור connected to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נזיר may not drink wine, which comes from the vine. He is punishable once he drinks a רביעית. So the vine in the verse hints to the רביעית שיעור for a נזיר.

keyTerms.meaning: A quarter of a לוג, a standard liquid measure
A person who took a vow to avoid wine and grape products, among other things

phrases.english: Vine — the quantity of a quarter-log of wine for a nazirite.
phrases.notes: The amount for which a נזיר who drinks wine is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of species, moving from שעורה to גפן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The שיעור for a נזיר drinking wine is a רביעית, hinted to by גפן.

steps.title: The fig hints to the dried-fig size for carrying on שבת
steps.stepSummary: The verse's word תאנה hints to the כגרוגרת שיעור (the size of a dried fig), the amount of food that makes a person liable for carrying it out on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: Fig: the size of a dried fig, for carrying out on שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the שיעור hinted to by the word תאנה: the size of a dried fig, for the מלאכה of הוצאה on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person is liable for carrying food from one domain to another on שבת only if it is at least a גרוגרת. Since this measure is a type of fig, the word תאנה in the verse hints to it. With this, the גמרא has matched another species in the verse to a שיעור.

keyTerms.meaning: The size of a dried fig
The מלאכה of carrying from one domain to another on שבת

steps.whatToRemember: Each species in the verse hints to a שיעור. חטה is the אכילת פרס time, measured with wheat bread, for בית המנוגע. שעורה is a barley-sized bone of a מת. גפן is a רביעית of wine for a נזיר. תאנה is a גרוגרת for carrying on שבת.

phrases.english: Fig — a dried-fig bulk for carrying out on Shabbat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of species, moving from גפן to תאנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The שיעור for liability in carrying food on שבת is a גרוגרת, hinted to by תאנה.

steps.title: Pomegranate: the size of a hole that makes a homeowner's vessel broken
steps.stepSummary: The word רמון in the verse hints to the rule that a homeowner's vessels count as broken once they have a hole the size of a pomegranate.
steps.simpleTranslation: Pomegranate: as we learned in a משנה, 'All vessels of homeowners: their measure is pomegranates.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the list of hints from the verse. It explains that the word רמון (pomegranate) points to a known measurement from a משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A homeowner does not throw away a vessel just because it has a small hole. He keeps using it, so it stays a 'vessel' and can still become טמא. Only a hole the size of a pomegranate makes it truly broken. At that point it can no longer be טמא, and if it was טמא, it becomes טהור.

phrases.english: Pomegranate:
phrases.notes: The next word in the verse ארץ חטה ושעורה וגפן ותאנה ורמון.

phrases.english: as we learned in a Mishnah:
all vessels of homeowners,
phrases.notes: Wooden vessels in ordinary household use.

phrases.english: their measure is the size of pomegranates.
phrases.notes: A hole this large makes the vessel 'broken', so it is no longer able to be טמא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the word-by-word list of hints from the verse, after תאנה in step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Homeowners' vessels are considered broken (and so cannot be or stay טמא) when they have a hole the size of a pomegranate.

steps.title: Olive: a land whose measurements are olive-sized
steps.stepSummary: The phrase 'ארץ זית שמן' is read as 'a land whose measurements are all the size of an olive'.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'A land of olive oil (and honey)': a land all of whose measurements are olive-sized.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the next part of the verse. It reads 'ארץ זית' as teaching that the measurements of the land are כזית, olive-sized.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse repeats the word 'ארץ' before זית. This lets the teaching read it as a general statement about 'the land's measurements' rather than one single law. As worded here, it claims that all measurements are a כזית. The גמרא is about to question that wording.

phrases.english: 'A land of olive oil (and honey)':
a land all of whose measurements are olive-sized.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list with the next phrase of the verse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word זית hints that the measurements of the land are כזית.

steps.title: How can all measurements be olive-sized?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: we just listed many measurements that are not a כזית, so the claim that 'all' are a כזית cannot be right.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'All of its measurements'? Could that enter your mind?! There are those measurements we just said!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of the last step. It points out that it cannot be that every measurement is a כזית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list itself already includes other measures: the time of אכילת פרס (wheat bread), a barley grain of bone, a רביעית of wine, a dried fig on שבת, and a pomegranate-sized hole. So the word 'all' contradicts the very teaching it belongs to.

keyTerms.meaning: Could it enter your mind? (a strong objection)

phrases.english: 'All of its measurements'? Could that enter your mind?!
But there are these measurements that we just mentioned!
phrases.notes: אכילת פרס time, barley grain, רביעית, dried fig, pomegranate.

steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'שכל שיעוריה כזיתים' in step 7.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Internal contradiction: the same teaching has just listed several measurements that are not a כזית.

steps.title: Correction: most measurements are olive-sized
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא fixes the wording: the teaching means that most of the land's measurements are a כזית, not all of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: most of its measurements are olive-sized.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question by changing one word in the teaching, from 'all' to 'most'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Many halachic measurements really are a כזית. Examples include חלב, דם, פיגול, נותר, a dead body's flesh for אהל, and a נבלה. So 'most' fits the facts. It also leaves room for the other sizes already listed.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
that most of its measurements are olive-sized.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: The teaching said every measurement is a כזית.
steps.terutzMaskana: Most measurements are a כזית, and the others are the exceptions already listed.

steps.title: Honey: the large date, the measure for eating on יום הכפורים
steps.stepSummary: The word דבש hints to the measure of a large date, which is the amount of food that makes one liable for eating on יום הכפורים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Honey: the size of a large date, for יום הכפורים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reaches the last word of the verse, דבש. It ties it to the measurement for eating on יום הכפורים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'honey' of the verse is date honey, so the word points to a date. A person is liable for eating on יום הכפורים only if he eats the volume of a large date, an amount that settles one's mind.

keyTerms.meaning: The size of a large date

steps.confusionAlert: דבש in this verse is not bee honey. It means honey made from dates, which is why it hints to the size of a date.

phrases.english: Honey:
the size of a large date, for eating on Yom Kippur.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the list of hints after the side discussion about זית.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One is liable for eating on יום הכפורים only for the amount of a large date.

steps.title: So the measurements come from the Torah itself?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws the conclusion from the whole list: the measurements seem to come from a verse, so they are Torah law, against רב's teaching that they are הלכה למשה מסיני.
steps.simpleTranslation: Apparently, they are from the Torah!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sums up the full list of hints and turns it into a challenge. If a verse teaches all these sizes, they come from the written Torah.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This closes the challenge that started earlier. רב said שיעורין are a הלכה למשה מסיני, a tradition and not a written verse. The long list seems to show the opposite.

phrases.english: Apparently, they are from the Torah!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the completed list of hints (steps 2–10) to finish the challenge against רב's statement.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's statement that שיעורין are הלכה למשה מסיני.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A verse is shown to teach every measurement, so they seem to be Torah law, not an oral tradition.

steps.title: The measurements are a tradition from Sinai; the verse is only a hint
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof: the sizes are not actually written in the verse. They are הלכה למשה מסיני, and the verse is only an אסמכתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And can you really think so? Are the measurements written? Rather, they are a הלכה, and the verse is merely a support.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the challenge. It says the verse does not truly teach these sizes, so רב's statement stands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse only names seven foods. It never says 'a hole the size of a pomegranate' or 'a רביעית for a נזיר'. The real source is an oral tradition from סיני, and the Rabbis attached it to the verse as a memory aid (אסמכתא).

keyTerms.meaning: And can you really think so?
A הלכה למשה מסיני, an oral tradition
Merely a support or hint, not the true source

steps.whatToRemember: שיעורין are הלכה למשה מסיני. The verse 'ארץ חטה ושעורה...' is only an אסמכתא, a hint for remembering them, not their real source.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the important idea of an אסמכתא. A law can be linked to a verse even when it really comes from oral tradition. That is why such laws are not treated as directly 'written' Torah law.

phrases.english: And can you really think so?
Are the measurements written in the verse?
Rather, they are a halachah given to Moshe at Sinai,
and the verse is merely a support.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 11 and defends רב's statement.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reclassifying the source: the verse is an אסמכתא, not a true derivation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The verse teaches the measurements, so they are Torah law.
steps.terutzMaskana: The measurements are הלכה למשה מסיני, and the verse only hints to them.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: שיעורין are an oral tradition from סיני, and the verse is only a supporting hint.

steps.title: Blockages in immersion seem to come from the Torah
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב: the law that nothing may block the water during immersion is learned from a verse, so it is not a הלכה למשה מסיני.
steps.simpleTranslation: The laws of blockages are Torah law! As it is written: 'And he shall bathe his flesh in the water.' This teaches that nothing may come between him and the water.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the second item on רב's list, חציצין. It points out that a verse already teaches this law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב said חציצין are a הלכה למשה מסיני, meaning they come from oral tradition and not from a verse. But the verse says 'he shall bathe his flesh in the water,' which implies the water must touch his flesh directly. If the verse teaches the law, there seems to be no need for an oral tradition.

keyTerms.meaning: Blockages: something that stops water from touching the body during immersion

phrases.english: Blockages are Torah law!
phrases.notes: This is a challenge to רב's list.

phrases.english: As it is written: 'And he shall bathe his flesh in the water,'
that nothing should block
between him and the water!
phrases.notes: The water must touch 'his flesh' directly.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same kind of attack as step 11, now aimed at the next item on רב's list, חציצין.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's statement that חציצין are a הלכה למשה מסיני
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A verse already requires the water to touch the flesh directly, so the law has a Torah source and does not need an oral tradition.

steps.title: The tradition is about blockages in the hair
steps.stepSummary: The verse covers the body. The oral tradition from Sinai teaches about blockages in the hair, following רבה בר בר חנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the הלכה came, it came about his hair, as רבה בר בר חנה taught. For רבה בר בר חנה said: one hair tied in a knot blocks. Three hairs tied together do not block. Two, I do not know.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the verse teaches about the skin. The הלכה למשה מסיני teaches a separate detail, blockages in the hair.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse says 'his flesh,' so it only clearly covers the body itself. Hair is not flesh, so the rule about knotted hair needs the oral tradition. A single knotted hair can be tied tight enough to keep water out. Three hairs cannot be tied that tightly, and רבה בר בר חנה was unsure about two.

keyTerms.meaning: The הלכה, here meaning the הלכה למשה מסיני
I do not know (the law is left undecided)

phrases.english: When the tradition came, it came for his hair,
phrases.notes: The oral tradition adds a law the verse did not cover.

phrases.english: in line with Rabba bar bar Ḥana.
For Rabba bar bar Ḥana said:
One hair tied in a knot blocks,
phrases.notes: It can be knotted tightly enough to keep water out.

phrases.english: three hairs knotted together do not block,
phrases.notes: They cannot be tied tightly enough to keep water out.

phrases.english: two, I do not know.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 13 by giving the tradition a different job.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the subject: the verse covers one area and the tradition covers another
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The tradition and the verse both teach the same basic blockage law, so the tradition is unnecessary.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse covers the skin. The הלכה למשה מסיני covers the hair, as taught by רבה בר בר חנה.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up: one knotted hair DOES block, but three DON'T. The more hairs in the knot, the less tightly it can be tied.

steps.title: Hair is also included in the verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the hair rule also comes from the verse, because the extra word אֶת includes the hair.
steps.simpleTranslation: His hair is also Torah law! As it is written: 'And he shall bathe אֶת his flesh in the water.' The word אֶת includes whatever is attached to his flesh. And what is that? His hair!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 14. It shows that hair is also learned from the same verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse could have said only 'his flesh,' but it adds the extra word אֶת. That extra word includes something connected to the flesh, which is the hair. So the hair rule also has a Torah source, and the tradition is still left without a job.

keyTerms.meaning: A small Hebrew word that is often read as including something extra
That which is attached to / secondary to

phrases.english: His hair is also Torah law,
as it is written: 'And he shall bathe his flesh in the water,'
phrases.notes: The focus is now on the word אֶת.

phrases.english: the word אֶת includes what is attached to his flesh,
and what is that? His hair!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 14 with the same kind of attack used in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the hair rule is the job of the הלכה למשה מסיני
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The extra word אֶת in the verse includes the hair, so hair also has a Torah source.

steps.title: A new answer based on רבי יצחק begins
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a new answer: the tradition teaches the law of רבי יצחק. His words continue on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the הלכה came, it came for the teaching of רבי יצחק. For רבי יצחק said:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא starts a new answer and introduces רבי יצחק, whose actual teaching appears on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since both skin and hair have a source in the verse, the tradition must be teaching something else. The גמרא says it teaches the point made by רבי יצחק. We have to read on to learn what that point is.

keyTerms.meaning: For the teaching of רבי יצחק

phrases.english: When the tradition came, it came for the teaching of Rabbi Yitzḥak.
phrases.notes: A new job for the הלכה למשה מסיני.

phrases.english: For Rabbi Yitzḥak said:
phrases.notes: His statement continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 15 by giving the tradition yet another job.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moving the tradition to a different law
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The tradition teaches about hair, but hair is already in the verse.
steps.terutzMaskana: The tradition teaches רבי יצחק's law, which is explained on the next amud.
steps.confusionAlert: This step is not finished. The real content of the answer, רבי יצחק's statement, comes on the next amud.
